aos.name: Unit 1 AoS 1 · How do the structures of materials explain their properties?

topics.title: Atoms, isotopes and electron configuration
points: Protons (+1, mass 1) and neutrons (0, mass 1) are in the nucleus; electrons (−1, almost no mass) are in shells.
Atomic number \(Z\) = protons. Mass number \(A\) = protons + neutrons, so neutrons \(= A - Z\).
Isotopes have the same number of protons but different numbers of neutrons.
Relative atomic mass is the weighted mean of an element’s isotopes on the carbon-12 = 12 scale.
Shell n holds up to 2n² electrons (2, 8, 18, 32). Subshells: s holds 2, p 6, d 10. Fill order 1s 2s 2p 3s 3p 4s 3d.
Exceptions: Cr is [Ar] 3d⁵ 4s¹ and Cu is [Ar] 3d¹⁰ 4s¹. Transition metals lose 4s electrons before 3d.
topics.explain: Explain why sodium-23 and sodium-24 are the same element but have different masses.

qs.q: How many neutrons are in an atom of \({}^{37}\mathrm{Cl}\) (\(Z = 17\))?
Which is the subshell configuration of a sulfur atom (\(Z = 16\))?
Chlorine is \(75.8\%\) Cl-35 (\(34.97\)) and \(24.2\%\) Cl-37 (\(36.97\)). Calculate its relative atomic mass.
qs.e: Multiply each isotopic mass by its fractional abundance and add.

qs.q: How many protons, neutrons and electrons are in \({}^{39}\mathrm{K}^{+}\) (\(Z = 19\))?
qs.e: A \(+1\) ion has lost one electron: \(19 - 1 = 18\) electrons.

qs.q: Why do elements produce line emission spectra?
qs.a: Electrons absorb energy and jump to higher energy levels. When they fall back they emit light with exact energies (the differences between levels), so only certain wavelengths appear.
qs.e: Each element has its own set of energy levels, so its spectrum is a fingerprint (flame tests).

p: Almost all the mass of an atom is in its tiny nucleus; the electrons occupy the space around it and decide how the atom bonds. Because the number of protons fixes the element, changing the number of neutrons gives a different isotope of the same element, and changing the number of electrons gives an ion.
Isotopes of an element have the same chemical properties because they have the same electron arrangement. They differ in mass, and some are radioactive.

Masses are measured relative to carbon-12, which is given a mass of exactly 12. A mass spectrometer separates the isotopes of an element and gives the relative isotopic mass and percentage abundance of each. The relative atomic mass on the periodic table is the weighted mean.
\[A_r = \frac{\sum(\text{relative isotopic mass} \times \%\ \text{abundance})}{100}\]
Chlorine is 75.8% chlorine-35 (mass 34.97) and 24.2% chlorine-37 (mass 36.97).
\(A_r = \dfrac{34.97 \times 75.8 + 36.97 \times 24.2}{100} = 35.45\). The answer sits closer to 35 because that isotope is more abundant; use this as a check.

The shell model explains group trends, but it cannot explain why the fourth shell starts filling before the third is full. The Schrödinger model does: shells are divided into subshells (s, p, d, f) made of orbitals, each orbital holding at most two electrons. Subshells fill in order of increasing energy: 1s, 2s, 2p, 3s, 3p, 4s, 3d, 4p.

The 4s subshell is lower in energy than 3d, so it fills first. When transition metals form ions, the 4s electrons are lost first. Example: Fe is 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s² 3p⁶ 3d⁶ 4s², and Fe²⁺ is 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s² 3p⁶ 3d⁶.

Writing 3d before 4s is filled for potassium and calcium. Forgetting the chromium and copper exceptions. Giving an electron configuration for an ion with the neutral atom’s electron count. An excited-state configuration has an electron in a higher subshell than expected; it is not a different element.

topics.title: Periodic table trends
points: Period = number of occupied shells. Group = same number of valence electrons, so similar chemistry.
\(\text{Core charge} = \text{protons} - \text{inner-shell electrons}\). It increases across a period and stays the same down a group.
Across a period: atomic radius decreases, electronegativity and first ionisation energy increase, metallic character decreases.
Down a group: an extra shell, so radius increases, electronegativity and ionisation energy decrease, metallic character increases.
Metals get more reactive down a group; non-metals get less reactive down a group.
topics.explain: Use core charge to explain why fluorine is more electronegative than oxygen.

qs.q: Which has the largest atomic radius?
qs.e: Radius decreases across period 3 as core charge rises, so Na is largest.

qs.q: What is the core charge of a chlorine atom?
Explain why potassium is more reactive than sodium.
qs.a: Potassium’s valence electron is in a shell further from the nucleus (4th vs 3rd) with the same core charge, so it is held less strongly and lost more easily.

qs.q: Going down group 17, electronegativity…
qs.e: Valence electrons are further from the nucleus, so bonding electrons are attracted less.

p: Nearly every trend can be explained with two factors: core charge (how strongly the nucleus pulls on the valence electrons) and the distance of the valence shell from the nucleus. Across a period the core charge rises while the valence shell stays the same, so valence electrons are held more tightly. Down a group the core charge stays the same while the number of shells rises, so valence electrons are further away and held less tightly.

Atomic radius: decreases across a period (stronger pull draws the shell in) and increases down a group (more shells). Electronegativity, the ability of an atom to attract electrons in a bond: increases across, decreases down. First ionisation energy, the energy needed to remove one electron from an atom in the gas phase: increases across, decreases down. Metallic character: decreases across, increases down.

Metals react by losing electrons, so the more easily they lose them the more reactive they are: reactivity increases down group 1. Non-metals react by gaining electrons, so the more strongly they attract them the more reactive they are: reactivity decreases down group 17. Fluorine is the most reactive non-metal.
Explain why sodium has a larger atomic radius than chlorine.

Both have three occupied shells. Sodium has a core charge of +1 (11 − 10) and chlorine +7 (17 − 10). Chlorine’s valence electrons are attracted more strongly to the nucleus, so they are held closer, giving a smaller radius.

Some elements are in short supply or hard to obtain, such as helium, phosphorus, rare-earth elements and post-transition metals and metalloids used in electronics. Recycling them supports a circular economy, in which materials are kept in use for as long as possible instead of being mined, used once and thrown away.
Saying “more protons” alone; you must also mention the shell or shielding. Saying “more electrons means bigger” across a period. Explaining a trend by restating it.

topics.title: Covalent bonding, shapes and polarity
points: A covalent bond is a shared pair of electrons between non-metal atoms. Double and triple bonds share 2 or 3 pairs.
Lewis structures: count valence electrons, put the least electronegative atom (never H) in the centre, add bonds, then lone pairs.
VSEPR: electron groups repel. 2 groups linear 180°; 3 trigonal planar 120°; 4 tetrahedral 109.5°; 4 with 1 lone pair pyramidal; 4 with 2 lone pairs V-shaped.
A polar bond joins atoms of different electronegativity. A molecule is polar only if its shape is uneven (H₂O, NH₃); symmetrical molecules cancel out (CO₂, CH₄).
Forces between molecules: dispersion (all molecules, grows with size) < dipole–dipole (polar) < hydrogen bonding (H on N, O or F).
Covalent network lattices: diamond (4 bonds each, very hard, no conduction), graphite (3 bonds each, delocalised electrons conduct, layers slide).
topics.explain: Explain why water boils at 100 °C but methane boils at −162 °C.

qs.q: What is the shape of an ammonia (NH₃) molecule?
qs.e: 4 electron groups, 1 lone pair: trigonal pyramidal, about 107°.

qs.q: Which molecule is non-polar even though it has polar bonds?
qs.e: CO₂ is linear, so the two C=O dipoles cancel.

qs.q: Which intermolecular force exists between all molecules?
qs.e: Temporary dipoles form in every molecule.

qs.q: Why does graphite conduct electricity but diamond does not?
qs.a: In graphite each carbon bonds to 3 others, leaving one delocalised electron per atom free to move. In diamond all 4 valence electrons are in bonds, so no charged particles can move.

qs.q: When water boils, what is broken: covalent bonds or hydrogen bonds?
qs.a: Hydrogen bonds between molecules. The O–H covalent bonds inside each molecule stay intact.

p: A reliable order of working: count valence electrons, draw the Lewis structure, count electron groups around the central atom (a lone pair, single bond, double bond or triple bond each count as one group), name the shape from the positions of the atoms, then decide polarity.

Four groups with no lone pairs give a tetrahedral shape (CH₄, 109.5°). Four groups with one lone pair give a pyramidal shape (NH₃). Four groups with two lone pairs give a bent or V-shape (H₂O). Three groups give trigonal planar (BF₃). Two groups give linear (CO₂). Lone pairs repel more strongly than bonding pairs, which squeezes the bond angles slightly.

A bond is polar when the two atoms differ in electronegativity; the more electronegative atom carries a partial negative charge. A molecule is polar only if the bond dipoles do not cancel. Symmetrical molecules such as CO₂ and CCl₄ have polar bonds but are non-polar overall. Asymmetrical molecules such as H₂O, NH₃ and CHCl₃ are polar.

Melting and boiling a molecular substance breaks the forces between molecules, not the covalent bonds inside them. Dispersion forces act between all molecules and get stronger with more electrons and a larger surface area. Dipole–dipole forces act between polar molecules. Hydrogen bonds are especially strong dipole–dipole attractions that occur when hydrogen is bonded to N, O or F and is attracted to a lone pair on N, O or F of a neighbouring molecule.
Why does water (18 g mol⁻¹) boil at 100 °C while methane (16 g mol⁻¹) boils at −162 °C?

The molecules have similar numbers of electrons, so dispersion forces are similar. Methane is non-polar and has only dispersion forces. Water is polar with O–H bonds, so it forms hydrogen bonds between molecules, which need much more energy to overcome.

In covalent network lattices the atoms are held by covalent bonds throughout. Diamond: each carbon bonds to four others, so it is extremely hard with no free electrons. Graphite: each carbon bonds to three others in layers, leaving one delocalised electron per atom, so it conducts; the layers are held by weak dispersion forces and slide, so it is soft and a lubricant.

Saying covalent bonds break when a molecular substance boils. Calling a molecule polar because it has polar bonds without checking symmetry. Claiming hydrogen bonding for any molecule that contains H.

topics.title: Metals
points: Metallic bonding: a lattice of cations in a sea of delocalised valence electrons, held by electrostatic attraction.
Properties: conduct (free electrons), malleable and ductile (layers slide, electrons still hold them), lustrous, high melting points.
Work hardening (cold) gives small crystals: harder, brittle. Annealing (heat, cool slowly): large crystals, softer. Quenching (cool fast): hard, brittle. Tempering reheats gently: tough.
Alloys: substitutional (similar-sized atoms, brass) or interstitial (small atoms such as C in steel). Both stop layers sliding.
Reactive metals: metal + water → hydroxide + H₂. Recycling metals saves energy and supports a circular economy.
topics.explain: Use the metallic bonding model to explain why metals bend instead of shattering.

qs.q: Which treatment makes a metal softer and more malleable?
qs.e: Slow cooling grows large crystals with fewer boundaries.

qs.q: Why does steel (iron with carbon) resist bending more than pure iron?
qs.a: Small carbon atoms sit in gaps between iron cations (interstitial alloy), disrupting the layers so they cannot slide easily.

qs.q: Metals conduct electricity because…
o: their ions move through the lattice
qs.e: Cations stay fixed; the electrons carry charge.

p: Metal atoms lose their valence electrons into a shared “sea”. The lattice is held together by electrostatic attraction between the positive ions and the delocalised electrons. This attraction is strong and acts in all directions, which explains the usual properties.

Conductivity of electricity: delocalised electrons are free to move toward a positive terminal. Conductivity of heat: the electrons carry kinetic energy quickly through the lattice. Malleability and ductility: layers of cations can slide without breaking the bonding, because the sea of electrons still holds them. Lustre: free electrons reflect light. High melting point: strong attraction needs a lot of energy to overcome.
The model does not explain why metals differ so much in melting point, density or magnetism, or why some are much more reactive than others.

The reactivity series ranks metals by how easily they are oxidised. Reactive metals (K, Na, Ca) react with cold water to give a hydroxide and hydrogen. Moderately reactive metals (Mg, Zn, Fe) react with acids to give a salt and hydrogen. Metals react with oxygen to form oxides. Unreactive metals (Cu, Ag, Au) do not react with dilute acids.
Example: Mg(s) + 2HCl(aq) → MgCl₂(aq) + H₂(g).

Alloying adds other atoms that disrupt the regular layers, so they slide less easily and the alloy is harder. Heat treatment changes crystal size: quenching (heating then cooling rapidly) gives small crystals, harder but brittle; annealing (cooling slowly) gives larger crystals, softer and more ductile; tempering (quenching then gentle reheating) reduces brittleness while keeping hardness.

Metals can be recycled repeatedly without losing their properties. Recycling aluminium uses a small fraction of the energy needed to extract it from ore, and it reduces mining and landfill. This is a clear example of a circular economy.
Saying metals conduct because “ions move”; in a solid metal only the electrons move. Describing delocalised electrons as “free atoms”.

topics.title: Ionic compounds and precipitation
points: Metals lose electrons (cations), non-metals gain them (anions), reaching noble-gas configurations. Ions form a 3D crystal lattice.
Hard, high melting point, brittle (shifted layers put like charges together). Conduct only when molten or dissolved.
Formulas balance charge: Al³⁺ + O²⁻ → Al₂O₃. Roman numerals show variable charge: copper(II) sulfate.
Learn: NH₄⁺, OH⁻, NO₃⁻, HCO₃⁻, CH₃COO⁻, SO₄²⁻, CO₃²⁻, PO₄³⁻.
SNAPE ions (sodium, nitrate, ammonium, potassium, ethanoate) are always soluble. CHOPS (carbonate, hydroxide, oxide, phosphate, sulfide) are usually insoluble.
Ionic equations leave out spectator ions: Ag⁺(aq) + Cl⁻(aq) → AgCl(s).
topics.explain: Explain why solid salt does not conduct but salt water does.

qs.q: What is the formula of calcium nitrate?
Which pair of solutions forms a precipitate when mixed?
Write the ionic equation for BaCl₂(aq) + Na₂SO₄(aq).
qs.e: Na⁺ and Cl⁻ are spectator ions.

qs.q: Ionic solids are brittle because…
o: a shift lines up like charges, which repel

qs.q: What is the formula of iron(III) oxide?
qs.e: Fe³⁺ and O²⁻: swap and simplify, 2 : 3.

p: When a metal reacts with a non-metal, electrons transfer from the metal to the non-metal. The resulting cations and anions arrange in a three-dimensional lattice, held by strong electrostatic attraction between opposite charges in all directions. The formula is a ratio, not a molecule.

High melting point: strong attraction throughout the lattice. Hard but brittle: a force that shifts a layer brings like charges next to each other, and repulsion shatters the crystal. Does not conduct as a solid: ions are fixed in place. Conducts when molten or dissolved: ions are free to move.

Balance the total positive and negative charge. Calcium phosphate: Ca²⁺ and PO₄³⁻ need three calcium ions (+6) and two phosphate ions (−6), giving Ca₃(PO₄)₂. Use brackets when there is more than one polyatomic ion. For transition metals give the charge in Roman numerals: iron(III) oxide is Fe₂O₃.

A precipitation reaction occurs when two solutions are mixed and one combination of ions forms an insoluble compound. Use a solubility table. Always soluble: compounds of Na⁺, K⁺, NH₄⁺, NO₃⁻ and CH₃COO⁻. Most chlorides, bromides and iodides are soluble except those of Ag⁺ and Pb²⁺. Most sulfates are soluble except those of Ba²⁺, Pb²⁺ and Ca²⁺ (slightly). Most carbonates, phosphates, sulfides and hydroxides are insoluble.
Solutions of lead(II) nitrate and potassium iodide are mixed.

Possible products: lead(II) iodide and potassium nitrate. Nitrates are soluble; PbI₂ is insoluble. Full equation: Pb(NO₃)₂(aq) + 2KI(aq) → PbI₂(s) + 2KNO₃(aq). Ionic equation: Pb²⁺(aq) + 2I⁻(aq) → PbI₂(s). K⁺ and NO₃⁻ are spectator ions.
Leaving out state symbols, which carry the meaning in a precipitation equation. Writing PbI instead of balancing charges. Saying an ionic solid conducts because it “has electrons”.

topics.title: Dissolving and chromatography
points: Like dissolves like. Ionic solids dissolve in water through ion–dipole attractions; small polar molecules form hydrogen bonds with water.
Chromatography separates by competition between adsorbing to the stationary phase and dissolving in the mobile phase.
\[R_f = \frac{\text{distance moved by component}}{\text{distance moved by solvent front}}\] It is always between \(0\) and \(1\).
Components that dissolve well in the mobile phase travel further; strongly adsorbed ones stay low.
Identify substances by comparing Rf values with standards under identical conditions. Baseline in pencil, above the solvent.
topics.explain: Explain why two dyes separate on a TLC plate.

qs.q: A spot moves \(3.0\ \mathrm{cm}\) while the solvent front moves \(12.0\ \mathrm{cm}\). Find \(R_f\).
A component with a high Rf is…
o: strongly adsorbed to the stationary phase
more attracted to the mobile phase

qs.q: Why is the baseline drawn in pencil?
o: Ink would dissolve and run with the solvent

p: A solute dissolves when the attractions between solute and solvent particles are strong enough to replace the solute–solute and solvent–solvent attractions. Polar and ionic substances tend to dissolve in polar solvents such as water; non-polar substances dissolve in non-polar solvents such as hexane.

Ionic solids dissociate: the lattice breaks up and each ion is surrounded by water molecules (ion–dipole attraction). Small polar molecules such as ethanol and glucose dissolve by forming hydrogen bonds with water. Acids such as HCl ionise: they react with water to form ions.

All chromatography has a stationary phase that stays put and a mobile phase that moves through or over it. Components are continually adsorbing onto the stationary phase and desorbing back into the mobile phase. A component that is strongly attracted to the stationary phase spends more time stuck and moves slowly; one that is more soluble in the mobile phase moves quickly.
In paper and thin-layer chromatography the stationary phase is polar. With a less polar solvent, polar components travel a shorter distance and have lower Rf values.
A spot moves 3.2 cm from the origin while the solvent front moves 8.0 cm.
\(R_f = \dfrac{3.2}{8.0} = 0.40\). Rf has no units and is always between 0 and 1. It is only comparable when the stationary phase, solvent and temperature are the same.

Draw the origin line in pencil, because ink would dissolve and run. Keep the origin above the solvent level, or the sample dissolves into the solvent pool. Cover the container so the solvent does not evaporate from the paper. Mark the solvent front as soon as the paper is removed.

Measuring from the bottom of the paper instead of from the origin. Writing “absorb” for “adsorb”: adsorption is sticking to a surface. Saying a single spot proves purity; two substances may have the same Rf in that solvent.

aos.name: Unit 1 AoS 2 · How are materials quantified and classified?

topics.title: The mole and formulas
points: One mole \(= 6.02 \times 10^{23}\) particles (Avogadro’s constant, \(N_A\)).
Molar mass \(M\) (\(\mathrm{g\ mol^{-1}}\)) equals the relative mass from the periodic table.
\(n = \dfrac{m}{M}\) and \(n = \dfrac{N}{N_A}\)
\[\%\ \text{by mass} = \frac{\text{mass of element in 1 mol}}{M} \times 100\]
Empirical formula: grams in 100 g → divide by M → divide by the smallest → whole-number ratio.
Molecular formula \(=\) empirical formula \(\times \dfrac{M(\text{compound})}{M(\text{empirical formula})}\)
topics.explain: Explain the difference between an empirical and a molecular formula using glucose.

qs.q: How many moles are in \(10.0\ \mathrm{g}\) of NaOH (\(M = 40.0\ \mathrm{g\ mol^{-1}}\))?
How many molecules are in 0.50 mol of water?
A hydrocarbon is 85.7% C and 14.3% H. Find its empirical formula.
What is the percentage by mass of hydrogen in water?
A compound has empirical formula \(\mathrm{CH_2O}\) and \(M = 180\ \mathrm{g\ mol^{-1}}\). What is its molecular formula?

p: Atoms are too small to count, so chemists weigh them. The mole links the mass you can measure to the number of particles that react. One mole of any substance contains the same number of particles, and its mass in grams equals its relative mass.

\(n = \dfrac{m}{M}\) converts between mass and moles. \(n = \dfrac{N}{N_A}\) converts between number of particles and moles. For a compound, the subscripts give mole ratios of atoms: 1 mol of \(\mathrm{H_2SO_4}\) contains 2 mol of H atoms, 1 mol of S atoms and 4 mol of O atoms.
How many oxygen atoms are in 4.9 g of H₂SO₄ (M = 98.1 g mol⁻¹)?

\(n(\mathrm{H_2SO_4}) = \dfrac{4.9}{98.1} = 0.050\ \mathrm{mol}\). \(n(\mathrm{O}) = 4 \times 0.050 = 0.20\ \mathrm{mol}\). \(N(\mathrm{O}) = 0.20 \times 6.02 \times 10^{23} = 1.2 \times 10^{23}\) atoms.

notes.h: Worked example: empirical and molecular formula
p: A compound is 40.0% C, 6.7% H and 53.3% O by mass, with molar mass 180 g mol⁻¹.

In 100 g: \(n(\mathrm{C}) = \dfrac{40.0}{12.0} = 3.33\), \(n(\mathrm{H}) = \dfrac{6.7}{1.0} = 6.7\), \(n(\mathrm{O}) = \dfrac{53.3}{16.0} = 3.33\). Divide by the smallest: 1 : 2 : 1, so the empirical formula is \(\mathrm{CH_2O}\) (30 g mol⁻¹). \(180 \div 30 = 6\), so the molecular formula is \(\mathrm{C_6H_{12}O_6}\).

Rounding ratios such as 1.5 or 1.33 to a whole number: multiply all values by 2 or 3 instead. Using atomic number in place of molar mass. Forgetting that diatomic elements (H₂, N₂, O₂, F₂, Cl₂, Br₂, I₂) have a molar mass twice the atomic value. Giving too many or too few significant figures: match the data.

topics.title: Organic compounds
points: Alkanes CₙH₂ₙ₊₂ (-ane), alkenes CₙH₂ₙ (-ene, C=C), alkynes (-yne, C≡C), haloalkanes (chloro- etc.), alkanols (-ol, –OH), carboxylic acids (-oic acid, –COOH).
Prefixes: meth, eth, prop, but, pent, hex, hept, oct, non, dec.
Name from the longest chain; number from the end nearest the functional group; branches as prefixes (2-methylpropane, but-2-ene, propan-1-ol).
Structural isomers: same molecular formula, different structure.
Longer chains: higher boiling point and viscosity, lower volatility. –OH and –COOH hydrogen-bond, so they boil higher.
Alkenes undergo addition across C=C; alkanes undergo substitution with halogens in UV light.
topics.explain: Explain why ethanol boils much higher than propane even though their molar masses are similar.

qs.q: What is the name of CH₃CH(CH₃)CH₂CH₃?
qs.e: Longest chain is 4 C with a methyl on carbon 2.

qs.q: Which general formula belongs to alkenes?
What type of reaction occurs when ethene reacts with bromine?
qs.a: Addition: Br₂ adds across the double bond to form 1,2-dibromoethane.

qs.q: Butane and 2-methylpropane are…

notes.h: Why carbon forms so many compounds
p: Carbon has four valence electrons and forms four strong covalent bonds, including bonds to other carbon atoms in chains, branches and rings. A homologous series is a family of compounds with the same functional group and general formula, where each member differs from the next by CH₂. Members have similar chemical properties and a gradual change in physical properties.

Molecular formula: C₄H₁₀. Structural formula shows every bond. Semi-structural (condensed) formula lists each carbon with its attached atoms: CH₃CH₂CH₂CH₃. Skeletal formula shows the carbon chain as a zigzag line with hydrogens on carbon left out.

Find the longest carbon chain that contains the functional group. Number it from the end that gives the functional group or branch the lowest number. Name branches as alkyl groups (methyl, ethyl) in alphabetical order, with di- or tri- for repeats. Add the suffix: -ane, -ene, -yne, -ol (alcohol), -oic acid (carboxylic acid); haloalkanes use a prefix (chloro-, bromo-).
Example: CH₃CH(CH₃)CH₂CH₃ has a four-carbon chain with a methyl group on carbon 2: 2-methylbutane. CH₃CH₂CH(OH)CH₃ is butan-2-ol.

Alkanes and alkenes are non-polar: only dispersion forces, low boiling points that rise with chain length, insoluble in water. Branching lowers the boiling point because branched molecules pack less closely. Alcohols and carboxylic acids form hydrogen bonds, so they boil higher than alkanes of similar size, and the small ones dissolve in water. Solubility falls as the non-polar chain gets longer.

Combustion: complete combustion gives CO₂ and H₂O. Substitution: an alkane reacts with a halogen in UV light, replacing an H. Addition: an alkene reacts across the double bond, which is why alkenes decolourise bromine water and alkanes do not. Esters form when an alcohol reacts with a carboxylic acid.
Most organic chemicals are made from crude oil, a non-renewable source. Plant-based biomass is an alternative feedstock that can be renewed.
Not choosing the longest chain. Numbering from the wrong end. Drawing carbon with five bonds or leaving it with three. Calling the chain length by counting branches.

topics.title: Polymers and plastics
points: Addition polymers form from monomers with C=C (ethene → polyethene). No by-product.
Condensation polymers form from monomers with a functional group at each end, releasing a small molecule (usually water): polyesters, nylon, proteins.
LDPE: many branches, low density, soft. HDPE: few branches, chains pack closely, denser and more rigid.
Thermoplastics have no cross-links and soften on heating (recyclable). Thermosetting polymers have covalent cross-links and char instead of melting.
Isotactic polymers (side groups all on one side) pack best and have the highest melting points.
Sustainability: mechanical and chemical recycling, bioplastics, biodegradable plastics, circular economy.
topics.explain: Explain why a thermoplastic can be recycled by melting but a thermoset cannot.

qs.q: Which monomer can form an addition polymer?
qs.e: It needs a C=C double bond.

qs.q: HDPE is more rigid than LDPE because…
o: its chains pack more closely, giving stronger dispersion forces

qs.q: What small molecule is usually released in condensation polymerisation?
A polymer that chars instead of melting when heated is…

p: A polymer is a very large molecule made of many small repeating units called monomers. In addition polymerisation the double bond of each monomer opens and the monomers join end to end; nothing else is produced, so the polymer has the same empirical formula as the monomer. In condensation polymerisation each monomer has two functional groups; they join by forming ester or amide links and release a small molecule, usually water.

For an addition polymer, redraw the monomer with the double bond replaced by a single bond and with a bond extending from each of the two carbons. Put brackets around this repeating unit with a subscript n. Example: propene, CH₂=CH(CH₃), gives the repeating unit –CH₂–CH(CH₃)–. To find the monomer from a polymer chain, take two adjacent backbone carbons and restore the double bond.

Longer chains mean stronger dispersion forces in total, so higher melting point and strength. Branching keeps chains apart: low-density polyethene has many branches and is soft and flexible; high-density polyethene has few and is rigid. Crystalline regions, where chains line up, add strength and make the plastic opaque; amorphous regions are tangled and more transparent. Side groups matter: a bulky or polar side group changes stiffness and intermolecular forces.

Thermoplastics have only weak forces between chains, so they soften when heated and can be remoulded. Thermosetting polymers have strong covalent cross-links, so they char instead of melting and cannot be remoulded. Elastomers have occasional cross-links, so chains can stretch and spring back. Plasticisers are small molecules added between chains to make a plastic softer.

Most plastics are made from fossil fuels and persist in the environment, breaking into microplastics. Options include mechanical recycling (sorting, melting and remoulding, which works for thermoplastics), chemical or feedstock recycling (breaking the polymer back to monomers or fuel), bioplastics made from renewable biomass, and compostable plastics. A bioplastic is not automatically biodegradable, and a biodegradable plastic is not automatically made from plants.

Leaving a double bond in the repeating unit of an addition polymer. Forgetting the bonds that extend through the brackets. Saying thermosetting plastics have “stronger intermolecular forces”: their cross-links are covalent bonds.

aos.name: Unit 2 AoS 1 · How do chemicals interact with water?

topics.title: Properties of water
points: Hydrogen bonding between water molecules explains its unusual properties.
High specific heat capacity (\(4.18\ \mathrm{J\ g^{-1}\,{}^\circ C^{-1}}\)): oceans steady the climate. \(q = mc\Delta T\)
High latent heat of vaporisation (\(40.7\ \mathrm{kJ\ mol^{-1}}\)) and fusion (\(6.0\ \mathrm{kJ\ mol^{-1}}\)). \(q = nL\)
Ice is less dense than water because hydrogen bonds hold molecules in an open hexagonal lattice.
Cohesion gives surface tension; adhesion gives capillary action and wetting.
topics.explain: Explain why lakes freeze from the top down and why that matters for fish.

qs.q: How much energy heats \(250\ \mathrm{g}\) of water from \(20\,{}^\circ\mathrm{C}\) to \(80\,{}^\circ\mathrm{C}\)?
How much energy boils \(36.0\ \mathrm{g}\) of water at \(100\,{}^\circ\mathrm{C}\)?
Why does ice float?
o: Air bubbles are trapped in it
Hydrogen bonds hold molecules further apart in a hexagonal lattice
It has a lower molar mass

qs.q: On a heating curve, the flat sections show…
qs.e: Energy goes into breaking hydrogen bonds, not raising temperature.

p: Compared with other molecules of its size, water has very high melting and boiling points, a high heat capacity and a high latent heat. The cause is hydrogen bonding. Each water molecule has two O–H bonds and two lone pairs, so it can form up to four hydrogen bonds with neighbours. Breaking or loosening these requires a lot of energy.

Specific heat capacity is the energy needed to raise the temperature of 1 g of a substance by 1 °C. Water’s value of \(4.18\ \mathrm{J\ g^{-1}\,{}^\circ C^{-1}}\) is high, so water absorbs or releases a lot of energy for a small temperature change. This moderates the climate near oceans and makes water an effective coolant.
\[q = mc\Delta T\]

Latent heat is the energy needed to change the state of a substance at constant temperature. During melting or boiling the energy goes into overcoming forces between molecules, so the temperature does not rise. \(q = n \times L\) for molar latent heat, or \(q = m \times L\) for values given per gram. Evaporating sweat cools the body because the water takes its latent heat of vaporisation from the skin.
How much energy is needed to heat 250 g of water from 20.0 °C to 100.0 °C and then boil all of it? (Latent heat of vaporisation at 100 °C: 40.7 kJ mol⁻¹.)

Heating: \(q = 250 \times 4.18 \times 80.0 = 83\,600\ \mathrm{J} = 83.6\ \mathrm{kJ}\). Boiling: \(n = \dfrac{250}{18.0} = 13.9\ \mathrm{mol}\), so \(q = 13.9 \times 40.7 = 566\ \mathrm{kJ}\). Total ≈ 650 kJ. Boiling takes far more energy than heating.

As water freezes, each molecule forms four hydrogen bonds in a fixed, open hexagonal arrangement. This holds the molecules further apart than in the liquid, so ice is less dense and floats. Ice forming on top of lakes insulates the water below, which lets aquatic life survive winter.
Mixing joules and kilojoules. Using a temperature in place of a temperature change. Saying hydrogen bonds are the O–H bonds inside the molecule; they are the attractions between molecules.

topics.title: Acids, bases and pH
points: Brønsted–Lowry: acids donate H⁺, bases accept H⁺. Conjugate pairs differ by one H⁺.
Amphiprotic species can do both: H₂O, HCO₃⁻, HSO₄⁻, H₂PO₄⁻.
Strong acids ionise completely (HCl, HNO₃, H₂SO₄); weak acids partly (CH₃COOH). Strength is not concentration.
Acid + metal → salt + H₂. Acid + hydroxide or oxide → salt + water. Acid + carbonate → salt + water + CO₂.
\(\mathrm{pH} = -\log_{10}[\mathrm{H_3O^+}]\). \(K_w = [\mathrm{H_3O^+}][\mathrm{OH^-}] = 1.00 \times 10^{-14}\) at \(25\,{}^\circ\mathrm{C}\).
Each pH unit is a \(10\times\) change in \([\mathrm{H_3O^+}]\). Diluting a strong acid \(10\times\) raises pH by \(1\).
topics.explain: Explain the difference between a strong acid and a concentrated acid.

qs.q: What is the pH of \(0.010\ \mathrm{M}\) HCl?
Find the pH of \(0.010\ \mathrm{M}\) NaOH at \(25\,{}^\circ\mathrm{C}\).
What is the conjugate base of HSO₄⁻?
Write the products of hydrochloric acid reacting with calcium carbonate.
qs.a: Calcium chloride, water and carbon dioxide: 2HCl + CaCO₃ → CaCl₂ + H₂O + CO₂

qs.q: Which is amphiprotic?
qs.e: It can donate (→ CO₃²⁻) or accept (→ H₂CO₃) a proton.

p: An acid–base reaction is a proton transfer. The acid donates H⁺ and becomes its conjugate base; the base accepts H⁺ and becomes its conjugate acid. In HCl(aq) + H₂O(l) → H₃O⁺(aq) + Cl⁻(aq), HCl is the acid and Cl⁻ its conjugate base; H₂O is the base and H₃O⁺ its conjugate acid.
An amphiprotic substance can donate or accept a proton, depending on what it reacts with. Polyprotic acids can donate more than one proton, one step at a time: H₂SO₄ is diprotic, H₃PO₄ is triprotic.

Strength describes how completely an acid ionises in water. Concentration describes how much solute is dissolved per litre. They are independent: 0.001 M HCl is a dilute solution of a strong acid; 5 M ethanoic acid is a concentrated solution of a weak acid. At the same concentration a strong acid has a lower pH, conducts better and reacts faster than a weak acid.
\(\mathrm{pH} = -\log_{10}[\mathrm{H_3O^+}]\) and \([\mathrm{H_3O^+}] = 10^{-\mathrm{pH}}\). At 25 °C, \([\mathrm{H_3O^+}][\mathrm{OH^-}] = 1.0 \times 10^{-14}\).
Example 1: 0.020 M HCl. It is a strong monoprotic acid, so \([\mathrm{H_3O^+}] = 0.020\) and \(\mathrm{pH} = -\log(0.020) = 1.70\).

Acid + reactive metal → salt + hydrogen. Acid + metal hydroxide → salt + water. Acid + metal oxide → salt + water. Acid + metal carbonate → salt + water + carbon dioxide. Acid + metal hydrogencarbonate → salt + water + carbon dioxide. The ionic equation for a strong acid with a strong base is H⁺(aq) + OH⁻(aq) → H₂O(l).

Carbon dioxide dissolves in sea water to form carbonic acid, which lowers the ocean’s pH. The extra H₃O⁺ reacts with carbonate ions, leaving less carbonate for corals and shellfish to build calcium carbonate shells and skeletons.
Calling a weak acid “dilute”. Forgetting that 0.1 M H₂SO₄ gives more than 0.1 M H₃O⁺. Diluting an acid 10 times and saying the pH falls by 1: it rises by 1, and never past 7.

topics.title: Redox and galvanic cells
points: OIL RIG: oxidation is loss of electrons, reduction is gain. Oxidising agents are reduced.
Oxidation numbers: elements 0, simple ions = charge, O usually −2, H usually +1, total = charge.
Balance half equations in acid: atoms, then O with H₂O, H with H⁺, charge with e⁻.
More reactive metals displace less reactive metal ions: Zn + Cu²⁺ → Zn²⁺ + Cu.
Galvanic cell: anode = oxidation (−), cathode = reduction (+). Electrons flow anode → cathode through the wire.
The salt bridge moves ions (anions to the anode, cations to the cathode), never electrons.
topics.explain: Explain what the salt bridge does and what would happen without it.

qs.q: What is the oxidation number of Cr in Cr₂O₇²⁻?
In a Zn | Cu galvanic cell, the anode is…
Balance: MnO₄⁻ → Mn²⁺ (acidic solution).
What does the salt bridge carry?

p: A redox reaction is one in which electrons are transferred. Oxidation and reduction always happen together. The substance oxidised is the reducing agent (it causes the other to be reduced); the substance reduced is the oxidising agent.

Oxidation numbers are a bookkeeping tool: an increase means oxidation, a decrease means reduction. Rules in order: an element is 0; a monatomic ion equals its charge; hydrogen is +1 (except in metal hydrides); oxygen is −2 (except in peroxides); the numbers add to the overall charge.
Use KOHES: balance the Key element, add water to balance Oxygen, add H⁺ to balance Hydrogen, add Electrons to balance charge, add States.

Example: MnO₄⁻ to Mn²⁺. Mn is balanced. Add 4H₂O to the right for oxygen. Add 8H⁺ to the left for hydrogen. Charges: left +7, right +2, so add 5e⁻ to the left. MnO₄⁻(aq) + 8H⁺(aq) + 5e⁻ → Mn²⁺(aq) + 4H₂O(l).
To combine two half-equations, multiply them so the electrons lost equal the electrons gained, add them, and cancel anything that appears on both sides.

A more reactive metal is a stronger reducing agent and will displace a less reactive metal from a solution of its ions. Zinc placed in copper(II) sulfate solution: Zn(s) → Zn²⁺(aq) + 2e⁻ and Cu²⁺(aq) + 2e⁻ → Cu(s). The blue colour fades and a red-brown deposit forms. Copper placed in zinc sulfate solution does nothing.

If the two half-reactions are separated, the electrons must travel through a wire and can do work. The half-cell where oxidation happens is the anode and is negative, because electrons are released there. Electrons flow through the wire to the cathode, which is positive, where reduction happens. The salt bridge completes the circuit and keeps each half-cell electrically neutral; without it the reaction stops almost at once.

Rusting needs both oxygen and water. Iron is oxidised to Fe²⁺ and oxygen is reduced to OH⁻; further reactions give hydrated iron(III) oxide. Prevention: barriers such as paint or grease; galvanising with zinc; sacrificial protection, where a more reactive metal is attached and corrodes in place of the iron.
Calling the oxidised species the oxidising agent. Putting electrons on the wrong side: they are a product in oxidation and a reactant in reduction. Saying electrons flow through the salt bridge.

aos.name: Unit 2 AoS 2 · How are chemicals measured and analysed?

topics.title: Solubility and concentration
points: Solubility is the maximum mass dissolving in 100 g of water at a given temperature. Below the curve: unsaturated; on: saturated; above: supersaturated.
Most ionic solids are more soluble when hot; gases are less soluble when hot.
\(c = \dfrac{n}{V}\) (\(V\) in litres). Other units: \(\mathrm{g\ L^{-1}}\), ppm (\(\mathrm{mg\ L^{-1}}\)), % (m/v).
Dilution: \(c_1V_1 = c_2V_2\)
1.0 M MgCl₂ contains 1.0 M Mg²⁺ and 2.0 M Cl⁻.
topics.explain: Explain why a fizzy drink goes flat faster when warm.

qs.q: \(50.0\ \mathrm{mL}\) of \(2.00\ \mathrm{M}\) HCl is diluted to \(500.0\ \mathrm{mL}\). Find the new concentration.
What is [Cl⁻] in 0.30 M CaCl₂?
How many moles of NaCl are in \(250\ \mathrm{mL}\) of \(0.40\ \mathrm{M}\) solution?

p: A solution is unsaturated if more solute can dissolve at that temperature, saturated if no more can dissolve, and supersaturated if it holds more than the saturated amount (an unstable state that crystallises when disturbed). A solubility curve plots solubility against temperature. A point below the curve is unsaturated, on the curve saturated, above it supersaturated.

Example: the solubility of KNO₃ is 110 g per 100 g of water at 60 °C and 32 g per 100 g at 20 °C. A saturated solution in 50 g of water at 60 °C holds 55 g. Cooled to 20 °C it can hold only 16 g, so 55 − 16 = 39 g crystallises.

Molarity: \(c = \dfrac{n}{V}\) in mol L⁻¹ (M). Mass per volume: g L⁻¹, found from \(c(\mathrm{g\ L^{-1}}) = c(\mathrm{mol\ L^{-1}}) \times M\). Parts per million: mg of solute per kg of solution, or mg L⁻¹ for dilute aqueous solutions. Percentages: %(m/m) is grams per 100 g of solution, %(m/v) is grams per 100 mL, %(v/v) is mL per 100 mL.
What mass of NaOH (M = 40.0 g mol⁻¹) is needed to make 250.0 mL of 0.100 M solution?
\(n = cV = 0.100 \times 0.2500 = 0.0250\ \mathrm{mol}\). \(m = nM = 0.0250 \times 40.0 = 1.00\ \mathrm{g}\). Dissolve it in less than 250 mL of water in a volumetric flask, then make up to the mark.
What volume of 2.0 M HCl is needed to make 500 mL of 0.10 M HCl?
\(V_1 = \dfrac{c_2V_2}{c_1} = \dfrac{0.10 \times 500}{2.0} = 25\ \mathrm{mL}\). Add the acid to water and make up to 500 mL. Diluting changes the concentration but not the amount of solute.
Leaving volume in mL when using c = n ÷ V. Adding 500 mL of water to 25 mL instead of making the total up to 500 mL. Forgetting that ions from a salt may be at a multiple of the salt’s concentration.

topics.title: Titrations and stoichiometry
points: Stoichiometry: balanced equation → moles of known → mole ratio → convert to what is asked.
Limiting reagent: work out which reactant runs out first; it decides the amount of product.
Aliquot = pipette volume. Titre = burette volume. Concordant titres are within 0.10 mL.
Primary standard: pure, known formula, stable, does not absorb water.
Rinse burette and pipette with their own solution; rinse flasks with deionised water.
Burette rinsed with water → titre too large. Pipette rinsed with water → too few moles in aliquot.
topics.explain: Explain why rinsing the conical flask with water does not affect the result.

qs.q: \(20.00\ \mathrm{mL}\) of HCl needs \(18.50\ \mathrm{mL}\) of \(0.100\ \mathrm{M}\) NaOH. Find \(c(\mathrm{HCl})\).
What volume of H₂ forms at SLC from 2.43 g Mg? (Mg + 2HCl → MgCl₂ + H₂)
If the burette is last rinsed with water, the calculated concentration of the flask solution will be…
qs.e: The titrant is diluted, so a larger titre is needed.

qs.q: 4.0 g CH₄ reacts with 10.0 g O₂ (CH₄ + 2O₂ → CO₂ + 2H₂O). Which is limiting?
qs.e: 0.25 mol CH₄ needs 0.50 mol O₂ but only 0.3125 mol is present.

p: A titration finds an unknown concentration by reacting a measured volume of the unknown with a solution of accurately known concentration (a standard solution) until the reaction is just complete. The equivalence point is when the reactants have been mixed in exactly the mole ratio of the equation. The end point is when the indicator changes colour. A suitable indicator makes these nearly the same.

notes.h: Equipment and why it is used
p: Volumetric flask: makes a solution of accurately known volume. Pipette: delivers a fixed, accurate volume (the aliquot). Burette: delivers a variable, accurately measured volume (the titre). Conical flask: holds the reaction mixture and can be swirled without spilling. Titrations are repeated until three titres agree within 0.10 mL; these concordant titres are averaged.
A 20.00 mL aliquot of H₂SO₄ is titrated with 0.100 M NaOH. The average titre is 24.60 mL. Find the concentration of the acid.
Equation: H₂SO₄(aq) + 2NaOH(aq) → Na₂SO₄(aq) + 2H₂O(l).

Think about what the mistake does to the amount of substance in the flask or to the concentration in the burette. Burette rinsed with water: its solution is diluted, so a larger titre is needed. Pipette rinsed with water: the aliquot is diluted, so less reagent is in the flask and the titre is smaller. Conical flask rinsed with the aliquot solution: extra reagent is in the flask, so the titre is larger. Conical flask rinsed with water: no effect, because the amount of reagent is unchanged.
Systematic errors shift every result in the same direction and are not reduced by repeating. Random errors scatter results and are reduced by repeating and averaging.
5.0 g of Mg (M = 24.3) is added to 0.30 mol of HCl. Mg + 2HCl → MgCl₂ + H₂.
\(n(\mathrm{Mg}) = 0.206\ \mathrm{mol}\), which would need 0.412 mol of HCl. Only 0.30 mol is available, so HCl is limiting. \(n(\mathrm{H_2}) = \tfrac{1}{2} \times 0.30 = 0.15\ \mathrm{mol}\).
Ignoring the mole ratio. Averaging all titres including the rough one. Recording burette readings to one decimal place; record to two.

topics.title: Gases
points: Kinetic theory: gas particles move randomly, are far apart, have no forces between them and collide with the walls (pressure).
\(1\ \mathrm{atm} = 101.3\ \mathrm{kPa} = 760\ \mathrm{mmHg}\). \(T(\mathrm{K}) = T(^\circ\mathrm{C}) + 273\)
Boyle \(p_1V_1 = p_2V_2\); Charles \(\dfrac{V_1}{T_1} = \dfrac{V_2}{T_2}\); combined \(\dfrac{p_1V_1}{T_1} = \dfrac{p_2V_2}{T_2}\) (kelvin only).
\(pV = nRT\) with \(p\) in kPa, \(V\) in L, \(R = 8.31\ \mathrm{J\ K^{-1}\ mol^{-1}}\).
\(n = \dfrac{V}{V_m}\), where \(V_m = 24.8\ \mathrm{L\ mol^{-1}}\) at SLC (\(25\,{}^\circ\mathrm{C}\), \(100\ \mathrm{kPa}\)).
Greenhouse gases (CO₂, CH₄, H₂O, N₂O) absorb and re-emit infrared radiation.
topics.explain: Use kinetic theory to explain why heating a sealed can raises the pressure.

qs.q: A gas is \(3.00\ \mathrm{L}\) at \(27\,{}^\circ\mathrm{C}\) and \(100\ \mathrm{kPa}\). Find its volume at \(127\,{}^\circ\mathrm{C}\) and \(200\ \mathrm{kPa}\).
What volume does 0.200 mol of gas occupy at SLC?
At constant temperature, halving the volume of a gas will…
Use \(pV = nRT\) to find \(V\) for \(0.100\ \mathrm{mol}\) at \(25\,{}^\circ\mathrm{C}\) and \(100\ \mathrm{kPa}\).

p: Gas particles are in constant, rapid, random motion; they are far apart, so a gas is mostly empty space and can be compressed; forces between them are negligible; collisions are elastic; and the average kinetic energy is proportional to the temperature in kelvin. Pressure is caused by particles colliding with the walls of the container.

Smaller volume at constant temperature: particles hit the walls more often, so pressure rises. Higher temperature at constant volume: particles move faster and hit the walls harder and more often, so pressure rises. Higher temperature at constant pressure: the gas expands.

Temperatures must be in kelvin: \(T(\mathrm{K}) = T({}^\circ\mathrm{C}) + 273\). With \(R = 8.31\ \mathrm{J\ K^{-1}\ mol^{-1}}\), use pressure in kPa and volume in L. Standard laboratory conditions (SLC) are 25 °C and 100 kPa, where one mole of any gas occupies 24.8 L.
What volume does 4.00 g of CO₂ (M = 44.0 g mol⁻¹) occupy at 30 °C and 95.0 kPa?
What volume of CO₂ at SLC forms when 10.0 g of CaCO₃ (M = 100.1) reacts with excess acid? CaCO₃ + 2HCl → CaCl₂ + H₂O + CO₂.
\(n(\mathrm{CaCO_3}) = 0.0999\ \mathrm{mol} = n(\mathrm{CO_2})\). \(V = 0.0999 \times 24.8 = 2.48\ \mathrm{L}\).

The Sun’s radiation passes through the atmosphere and warms the Earth, which emits infrared radiation. Greenhouse gas molecules absorb that infrared radiation and re-emit it in all directions, including back toward the surface. This natural effect keeps the planet habitable. Human activity, mainly burning fossil fuels and agriculture, has raised the concentrations of CO₂, CH₄ and N₂O, producing the enhanced greenhouse effect and global warming.
Using °C in gas calculations. Using 24.8 L mol⁻¹ when the gas is not at SLC. Using it for liquids or solids.

topics.title: Analysis of salts
points: Sources of salts in water: minerals from rocks, heavy metals (Pb, Hg, Cd) from industry, organometallics such as methylmercury.
Gravimetric analysis: dissolve, precipitate with excess reagent, filter, wash, dry to constant mass, weigh, calculate.
A precipitate that is not fully dried makes the result too high.
Colorimetry and UV-visible spectroscopy: absorbance is proportional to concentration. Use standards to draw a calibration curve.
Choose a wavelength (or complementary-colour filter) where the substance absorbs most.
topics.explain: Explain why a precipitate must be dried to constant mass.

qs.q: \(0.466\ \mathrm{g}\) of \(\mathrm{BaSO_4}\) (\(M = 233.4\ \mathrm{g\ mol^{-1}}\)) is collected. Find the mass of sulfate ions.
In UV-visible spectroscopy, the unknown’s concentration is found from…
A precipitate is weighed while still damp. The calculated amount will be…

p: Water dissolves salts from rocks and soil, and human activity adds more: fertiliser run-off (nitrates and phosphates), mining and industry (heavy metals such as lead, mercury and cadmium), and irrigation (salinity). Analysis shows whether water is safe to drink or to release. Electrical conductivity gives a quick estimate of total dissolved salts, because more ions carry more current; it does not identify which ions are present.

Find the mass of a substance by converting it into a precipitate of known formula and weighing it. Steps: weigh the sample and dissolve it; add an excess of a reagent that precipitates the ion; filter; wash the precipitate with water to remove soluble impurities; dry and weigh it; repeat drying until the mass is constant.
A 2.00 g sample of fertiliser is dissolved and excess BaCl₂ is added. 1.17 g of BaSO₄ (M = 233.4) precipitates. Find the percentage of sulfate (M = 96.1) in the fertiliser.

Result too high: precipitate not dry; precipitate not washed, so soluble impurities remain; another ion also precipitated. Result too low: precipitate lost during transfer or through the filter; not enough reagent added; precipitate slightly soluble and washed with too much water.

A coloured solution absorbs light, and the more concentrated it is, the more it absorbs. Method: prepare a set of standard solutions of known concentration; measure the absorbance of each at a wavelength the substance absorbs strongly; plot a calibration curve of absorbance against concentration; measure the absorbance of the sample and read its concentration from the curve.
The sample’s absorbance must fall within the range of the standards. If it is too high, dilute the sample and multiply the result by the dilution factor.
Reading the calibration curve beyond the highest standard. Forgetting the dilution factor. Choosing light the same colour as the solution: a solution absorbs its complementary colour.
